speaker: Doctor
text: Welcome to the clinic. I understand you are experiencing episodes of dizziness and vertigo; to help me understand your condition better, how long do these episodes typically last, and do you feel any other symptoms like nausea or hearing changes?

speaker: Patient
text: 70-year-old woman. The patient presents with sudden episodes of dizziness that are position dependent. She describes experiencing a false sensation of motion and occasional spinning, indicative of vertigo. She denies any recent illnesses, injuries, or significant changes in health status, apart from age-related hearing loss (presbycusis).

speaker: Doctor
text:
Thank you for the details. Since your dizziness is triggered by changes in head position, have you noticed any new tinnitus, ear fullness, or difficulty hearing on one side?

REQUEST TEST: Audiometry; REQUEST IMAGES: MRI Internal_Auditory_Canals.

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Audiometry: Bilateral high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss, consistent with presbycusis. No sudden drops in hearing indicative of Meniere's disease or labyrinthitis. MRI Internal_Auditory_Canals: No evidence of central lesions, infarcts, or acoustic neuromas; findings consistent with the patient's age-related changes.

speaker: Doctor
text:
To confirm the duration of your episodes, do they typically last less than one minute and stop when you hold your head still? Also, have you experienced any recent neck pain, stiffness, or a "choking" sensation in the throat?

REQUEST TEST: Neck_Imaging (CT/MRI); REQUEST TEST: Thyroid_Function_Tests.

speaker: Doctor
text:
Since the neck imaging and thyroid function tests are normal, ruling out cervical and thyroid causes, do you experience any involuntary, rhythmic eye movements (nystagmus) when you look down at your feet or to the side?

REQUEST TEST: Ophthalmoscopy; REQUEST IMAGES: Videonystagmography (VNG).

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Ophthalmoscopy: Pupils equal and reactive, fundus normal, no retinal abnormalities. Videonystagmography: Normal vestibular response with the exception of response elicited during Dix-Hallpike maneuver, consistent with BPPV.

speaker: Doctor
text: DIAGNOSIS READY: Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV). The positive response to the Dix-Hallpike maneuver on VNG, combined with position-dependent vertigo and normal central/inner ear workup, confirms this diagnosis. I recommend starting canalith repositioning maneuvers (such as the Epley maneuver) to resolve the symptoms.
